name: Liam Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Liam. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I'm a lead framer on a housing association site at Millbrook, forty affordable homes in timber frame. My gang of five stands the wall panels, sets the joists and gets the roof trusses up before the bricklayers move in. Best part is standing on a finished first floor at four o'clock and seeing a house that wasn't there in the morning. Worst part is the pay, honestly, and the mud from October to March.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a terraced house with two mates from college, which keeps the rent down but not by enough. I send a bit home to my mum most months since my dad's back went. That's why I've never got more than a few weeks of money in the bank. I play five-a-side on Thursdays, and that's about my only spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: First picture. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, to be fair. I use one of those AI apps now and then to double-check a cut list, and it's handy, but it's not running the site. At five-a-side I'd say the hype people owe us all an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm stuck where I am. Nothing changing means nothing gets better either, and I'm still on less than the framers at the private developer up the road. I'm good at the job and I run a gang, and it doesn't show in the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on at Millbrook while the housing association has work, which is about another eighteen months. I'd ask our site manager, Gail, about a step up to assistant supervisor when the next phase starts. And I'd join the union properly instead of just meaning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Relieved about the robots, I suppose, but the money worries don't go anywhere. It's like getting good news from a doctor about the one thing you weren't worried about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said about eighteen months of work at Millbrook. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me checking the job boards. The housing association only funds one big site at a time round here, and the next one isn't confirmed. If it falls through, it's private developers or driving to the coast for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if a month goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money to my mum, and I hate that. Rent and the phone have to go out, so the thing I can actually skip is her two hundred. She'd say it's fine, but she'd be short on her heating.

say: I'd say AI turned out about how **I expected**: handy for a cut list, not running sites.
At five-a-side I'd say the **hype people** owe us an apology.
think: I think nothing changing leaves me **stuck on lower pay** than the private framers.
My real worry is that **Millbrook ends** in about eighteen months.
do: Keep leading the framing gang at **Millbrook** while the work lasts.
Ask Gail, the site manager, about **assistant supervisor** on the next phase.
Join the **union** properly instead of just meaning to.
feel: I feel **flat**: relieved about robots but still squeezed on money.
S0.quote: Nothing changing means nothing gets better either, and I'm still on less than the framers at the private developer up the road.
fieldNote: Liam's pressure is the **end of the site** in eighteen months, not AI.
He sends **two hundred a month** to his mum, which is the first thing cut in a bad month.
He already uses AI **now and then** for cut lists and treats it as ordinary.
He frames his hope around a **promotion** rather than a move.

steps.text: Keep running the framing gang at Millbrook until the site ends
Ask the site manager about an assistant supervisor role on phase two
Sign up as a full union member this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get social housing built faster, if the savings go into more homes and not profits. On site I'd tell the lads it hits the office before it hits us. I might put something online about using it to build more homes, because that's what I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly fine for me for a few years. The housing association's estimators and buyers would shrink, and Gail would be doing more of her planning on a laptop. My worry is that the next phase gets planned so tight that my gang loses a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the planning apps more, properly, not just for cut lists. I'd ask Gail if I can sit with her when they bring in the scheduling software, so I understand it before it's used on us. And I'd go to the union meetings and ask what they're doing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not bad. I'm the type to wait until something's proven, and this is getting proven around me. So I'd rather learn it while it's still my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your gang might lose a person. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sunil, who's our newest. He's fine on the tools but slow on the setting out, and a tighter programme would show that up. I'd try to keep him by pairing him with me on the hard bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be one of the ones saying it's a good thing, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of, yeah, if it gets more homes built. My cousins are still in a two-bed with three kids. If AI means councils can afford more housing sites, I'd be all for it, as long as we're the ones building them.

say: I'd say it could get **social housing** built faster if savings go into more homes.
I'd tell the lads it hits the **office first**, before the site.
think: I think I'm **mostly fine** for a few years, but the office shrinks.
My worry is a **tighter programme** that cuts one person from my gang.
do: Use the **planning apps** properly, not just for cut lists.
Sit with Gail when the **scheduling software** arrives, to learn it first.
Go to **union meetings** and ask what the plan is.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but not bad, and I'd rather learn it while it's **my choice**.
S1.quote: If AI means councils can afford more housing sites, I'd be all for it, as long as we're the ones building them.
fieldNote: Liam judges AI by whether it gets **more homes built**, tied to his cousins' crowded flat.
He'd learn the software early to **understand it before** it's used on his gang.
He worries about **Sunil**, the newest framer, under a tighter programme.
His steady streak shows: he waits until it's **proven around him**.

steps.text: Use the planning app for setting out and cut lists every week
Sit with the site manager when the scheduling software arrives
Raise the new software at the next union branch meeting
Pair with Sunil on setting out to keep him on the gang

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, fast, with a plan for workers and a plan for housing. I'd share union posts and sign whatever petition is going. At work I'd say we've got a few years yet on the tools, so don't walk off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I've got until about 2031 before a robot can stand a wall panel as well as my gang. The planning and ordering at Millbrook goes by 2028, so Gail's job changes first. I'd be 30, with no savings and my mum still needing help, so it's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn whatever software runs the site, because the person who can work with it lasts longer. I'd try to get on the timber frame factory course at the college, since the factory is where the robots will be and someone has to run them. And I'd cut the five-a-side and save that, small as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a path, but it's a narrow one. If I lose the footing, my mum loses her two hundred too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and the robots do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to move from the hammer to the screen, if I'm quick. The thinking jobs go first, so I can't jump to the office, there won't be one. I'd want to jump to the factory floor, running the panel machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm going back to college in the evenings and the money might be a bit less for a while. She'd tell me not to send her anything at all, and we'd argue. My dad would say a man with a trade is always fine, and I'd have to tell my dad that's not true any more.

say: I'd say government must **step in fast** with plans for workers and housing.
I'd tell the gang we have **a few years** on the tools, so don't walk off.
think: I think robots match my gang around **2031**, after planning goes in 2028.
At 30 with **no savings** and my mum relying on me, it's not great.
do: Learn whatever **site software** comes in, since that person lasts longer.
Start the **timber frame factory** course at college in the evenings.
feel: I feel **anxious**: there's a path, but a **narrow one**.
S2.quote: My dad would say a man with a trade is always fine, and I'd have to tell my dad that's not true any more.
fieldNote: Liam sees the factory floor as the **safer jump**, since the office goes first.
He uses the **three-year gap** to learn machines, not to wait.
His **mum's two hundred** a month raises the stakes of any income dip.
A telling moment: telling his father that **a trade isn't safe** any more.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening timber frame factory course at the college
Learn the new site scheduling software in the first months
Drop five-a-side and bank the fee each month
Sign union petitions for a public plan for site workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd say it at union meetings and on the group chat. I'd push for the housing association to train its own site staff on the new machines. To mates I'd say don't panic, but don't sit still either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is about right for me. The thinking side changes by 2031, robots around 2034, and I'd be 33 by then. That's enough time to get the factory qualification and some savings, if nothing else goes wrong at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools more on the job for planning and setting out, so I'm the person on site who gets the new stuff. I'd go to the college in the second year, once I'd seen which courses actually lead to jobs. I'd try to save a hundred a month, and keep sending my mum her money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the fast one. Five years lets me do things in the right order. I'd still feel the clock, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year to pick a course. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen lads pay for courses that led nowhere. My mate Owen did a drone surveying thing and never got a day's work from it. I want to see which ones the firms actually hire from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning your mum. Would any of this change if she didn't need help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, completely. I'd have savings, I could move to the city for a factory job, I could take a pay cut to train. With my mum needing me, I've got to keep the money coming every single month.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so let's use them, on the chat and at meetings.
I'd push the housing association to **train its own staff** on the machines.
think: I think five years is **about right** for me; I'd be 33 when robots come.
It's enough for a **factory qualification** and savings, if nothing goes wrong at home.
do: Use **AI tools** more for planning and setting out on site.
Pick a **college course** in year two, once I see which lead to jobs.
Save **a hundred a month** while still sending my mum her money.
feel: I feel **anxious** but steadier, because I can do things **in order**.
S3.quote: With my mum needing me, I've got to keep the money coming every single month.
fieldNote: Liam's steadiness shows in waiting to see which **courses lead to jobs**.
He cites Owen's **drone surveying course** that led nowhere as a warning.
His **mum's needs** are the real limit on retraining or moving.
Five years feels to him like time to act **in the right order**.

steps.text: Use the AI planning tools for setting out on every new plot
Choose and start a college course in the second year
Save a hundred a month in a separate account
Push the housing association to train its site staff on new machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this properly, so let's not waste it on arguing. I'd say it at the union and probably at the pub. I'd also say we should build as many homes as we can before the robots take over, because people need them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I can breathe. AGI by 2036 and robots around 2039 means I've got a decade of framing, and I'd be 37 when it really bites. My mum might be sorted by then, and I might have a bit put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep framing and keep using the apps, nothing dramatic. I'd ask Gail about the supervisor route, because that's the kind of job that might last longest on a robot site. I'd start saving properly, even fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say, but calm about the next few years. It's a long road and I can see most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sunil, the new lad, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's got ten good years, so learn every bit of the job, then learn the machines. He'd probably laugh at me. He thinks AI is just a thing on his phone that writes his texts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, honestly. With two years I'd be scrambling for courses, but with ten I'd go for the supervisor job first, then see. Slow and sure suits me.

say: I'd say ten years is **a real chance**, so let's not waste it on arguing.
We should build **as many homes** as we can before the robots take over.
think: I think I can **breathe**, with a decade of framing ahead.
I'd be **37** when it bites, maybe with savings and my mum sorted.
do: Keep **framing** and using the apps, nothing dramatic.
Ask Gail about the **supervisor route**, which may last longest on robot sites.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the end but **calm** about the next few years.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be scrambling for courses, but with ten I'd go for the supervisor job first, then see.
fieldNote: The long warning turns Liam from scrambling to **staying put** and planning.
He sees **supervisor roles** as the longest-lasting job on a robot site.
He'd tell young **Sunil** to master the trade, then the machines.
His mood eases because he hopes his **mum's needs** ease over a decade.

steps.text: Keep framing at Millbrook and using the planning app
Ask the site manager about the supervisor training route
Save fifty a week into a separate account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because the robots would reach framing when I'm 30 and I'd have no savings and my mum still relying on me. What would help is a paid evening course at the college for factory panel machines, and a housing association that trains its own builders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the homes themselves. Everyone talks about jobs, but if robots make building cheaper, I want those savings in council housing, not shareholders.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but if robots make building cheaper, I want those savings in council housing, not shareholders.
portrait: Liam is 27, a **lead framer** on a housing association site, on lower pay than private framers.
He shares a rented house and sends his **mum two hundred** a month, so savings stay thin.
He uses AI apps **now and then** and would learn new site software early.
He sees the **timber frame factory** as his safest jump if robots arrive soon.
Ten years' warning lets him **stay put** and aim for a supervisor job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: robots reach framing at **30**, with **no savings** and his mum relying on him.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid evening course** for factory panel machines at the college.
A housing association that **trains its own builders** for the new machines.
